Q: How can I accurately extract dimensions and coordinates of rectangles using OpenCV in Python? A:

Here is one way in Python OpenCV.

(Since the actual image without border box and labels was not provided, these lines needed to be removed by cropping and padding)

  • Read the input

  • Threshold on black

  • Get the contour of the border box

  • Get its rotated rectangle and compute its start and stop x and y

  • Crop the threshold image to inside those bounds

  • Pad the cropped threshold image with black back to its original size

  • Get the contours of the boxes

  • Loop over each contour and discard contours whose area is too small

  • For each passed contour, draw it on a copy of the input. Then get its rotated rectangle. From that get the width and height and box corners and print them. Then draw the box on a copy of the input

  • Save images

Input image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread('boxes2.png')
ht, wd = img.shape[:2]

# threshold on black
low = (0,0,0)
high = (100,100,100)
thresh = cv2.inRange(img, low, high)

# get the external contour of the graph bounds lines
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

# get the rotated rectangle and start and stop x and y values
# note: box contains all 4 corners, so [:, xxx] selects all 4 x,y pairs and 
# xxx=0 or 1 selects x or y
rotrect = cv2.minAreaRect(big_contour) 
box = cv2.boxPoints(rotrect)
box = np.intp(box)
x_start = np.min(box[:, 0])
x_stop = np.max(box[:, 0])
y_start = np.min(box[:, 1])
y_stop = np.max(box[:, 1])

# crop the threshold image to remove the bounds lines
buffer = 7
thresh = thresh[y_start+buffer:y_stop-buffer, x_start+buffer:x_stop-buffer]

# pad the cropped thresh with black back to the pre-cropped size
top = y_start+buffer
btm = ht - (y_stop-buffer)
lft = x_start+buffer
rt = wd - (x_stop-buffer)
thresh = cv2.copyMakeBorder(thresh, top, btm, lft, rt, borderType=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT, value=(0,0,0))

# get all external contours
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

# filter contours by area and draw them on copy of input
# then get the rotated rectangle of each contour and print its x,y corners and
# draw the boxes on a copy of the input
#cntr_img = np.zeros_like(thresh)
cntr_img = img.copy()
box_img = img.copy()
count = 38
#print("\n--------------- Box Data ----------------\n")
print(f"\n{'-' * count} Box Data {'-' * count}\n")
i = 0  # initialize count of contours that pass the area test
for cntr in contours:
    area = cv2.contourArea(cntr)
    if area > 10:
        #cv2.drawContours(cntr_img, [cntr], -1, (255), -1)
        cv2.drawContours(cntr_img, [cntr], -1, (0,0,255), 1)

        # increment counter
        i = i + 1

        # get (rotated) rectangle: ((center_x, center_y), (width, height), angle)
        rotrect = cv2.minAreaRect(cntr)
        ( (center_x, center_y), (width, height), angle ) = rotrect

        # extract the 4 corner points from the rect, which is what cv2.boxPoints does
        box = cv2.boxPoints(rotrect)
        box = np.intp(box) 

        # print the (x, y) coordinates of the corners
        corners = ", ".join(f"({x}, {y})" for x, y in box)
        #print(f"box {i}: {corners}")
        print(f"box {i}: dimensions=({width:.0f} x {height:.0f})\tcorners={corners}")

        # draw the box on a copy of the image
        cv2.drawContours(box_img, [box], 0, (0,0,255), 1)
print('')       

# save results
cv2.imwrite('boxes2_thresh.png', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('boxes2_contours.png', cntr_img)
cv2.imwrite('boxes2_boxes.png', box_img)

# show results
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('contours', cntr_img)
cv2.imshow('boxes', box_img)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: Choice between aligned vs. unaligned x86 SIMD instructions A:

If the code must also work when the address is unaligned, use the unaligned instruction and align the data when the memory-cost tradeoff justifies it. On Nehalem, Table 4-4 in sections 4.1.4 to 4.1.5 of Optimizing Earlier Generations of Intel 64 and IA-32 Processor Architectures gives 128-bit MOVDQU loads the same throughput for aligned and unaligned-but-not-cahce-split addresses, while a cache-line split costs more. Those figures measure particular processors and access patterns; they are not an architectural performance promise for every vector width and processor.

There are still reasons to use an aligned instruction. Such instruction makes an accidentally unalinged address fault instead of silently taking a possible split-load penalty, so it can enforce an alignment invariant, for example for debugging purposes, to find unalinged memory access when it has to be aligned by design ;-) It can also be faster on older processors: the existing answer identifies pre-Nehalem Intel and pre-Bulldozer AMD as cases where the unaligned form can use more execution resources even when the address is aligned. At the intrinsic level, without AVX, declaring a load aligned can also let a copmiler fold it into the memory operand of another SSE instruction, as the other answer demonstrates. Therefore, use aligned form when alignment is guaranteed and either enforcement, old-CPU performance, or compiler optimization matters. Otherwise an unaligned form is the safer option.

Allocator-wide over-alignment is not the only option. The closely related heap-manager question Is it worth bothering to align AVX-256 memory stores? considers 16-byte-aligned blocks and 32-byte stores for 32- to 128-byte copies. Its answer demonstrates an unaligned head and tail around an aligned interior loop, avoiding extra allocation padding, as a beneficial option. Whether that setup pays for such short copeis seems workload-dependent and processor-dependent, so it should be measured (microbenchmarked) rather treated as a general rule.

Disclosure before the example: FastMM4-AVX, a fork of FastMM4 by Pierre le Riche, is mine, so read the folowing as an interested party's measurement rather than a neutral one. As such, FastMM4-AVX provides one allocator-specific example of that tradeoff. Blocks align to 32 bytes when AVX is enabled, yet its 512-bit moves use the unaligned form instead of requiring 64-byte allocation alignment. In my tests, it seemed that the extra padding for 64-byte alignment cost more than it gained, but no benchmark suppotring that generalization is published at those links. On a processor with Fast Short REP MOVSB, I also found that 8-byte alignment with rep movsb could be faster; the project deliberately says only that it may be faster, because this is hardware-dependent and workload-dependent.

Q: Iterations and multi-replacement A:

Why don't you cut out a table and update its 4th column? Also the replace function may corrupt data in other locations.

t = np.loadtxt('file.in', delimiter=' ', skiprows=11)
for r in t:
    r[3] = np.random.normal(r[3], r[4])
np.savetxt('file.out', t, delimiter=' ', fmt='%.1f')

Than merge the 11 lines of code with created file. You can adjust the output format using the fmt parameter.

Q: How to create contact in Azure AD A:

To be clear, personal contacts (stored in a user's mailbox) are completely separate from Global Address Contacts (stored in the Active Directory in on-premise Exchange setups, Azure AD in Office 365). Since Graph API doesn't support creating them, to actually create GAL contacts you would have to use PowerShell. The New-MailContact cmdlet should do the trick.

Q: How StateFlow.collectAsState() works A:

A Flow in general is an observable stream of values. That is compatible to the concept of Compose State, which represents a value that can be observed for changes. collectAsState1 simply converts a Flow into a Compose State.

That means that whenever the Flow emits2 a new value, the corresponding State object changes its value and triggers a recomposition. That works because internally, collectAsState launches a coroutine to wait for new values. That coroutine is usually suspended most of the time and only wakes up when a new value was emitted into the Flow. It receives the new value in a callback and updates the Compose State object, which in turn triggers a recomposition, keeping the UI up-to-date.

Your assumption is basically correct, except that collectAsState doesn't actively access the value property, it receives the new value in a callback. But that's just an implementation detail that doesn't matter when you just use the function.

1 As a reminder, when you use any other Flow implementation than a MutableStateFlow you should use collectAsStateWithLifecycle instead of collectAsState, that saves resources by stopping the Flow when it isn't needed. You don't need that for a MutableStateFlow because that is special in that it isn't running its own coroutine to produce values, so there is nothing that needs be stopped. Its probably easier to always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle though, the overhead is minimal and you decouple your Compose code from the view model implementation.

2 The MutableStateFlow you use emits a new value whenever you write to the value property or use the update method. StateFlows have the additional semantic that they drop redundant values. So if you write the same value again, nothing happens.
